source: Lin et al. (2025) ZebraLogic: On the Scaling Limits of LLMs for Logical Reasoning
finding: Logic grid puzzles built as CSPs with known search-space size and Z3 conflict counts. Accuracy falls sharply as the CSP gets harder, for every model size. The authors call this the curse of complexity.
numbers: Overall puzzle accuracy: DeepSeek-R1 81.0, o1-preview 78.7, o1-mini 71.4, Sonnet 3.5 36.2, Llama-3.1-405B 32.6, GPT-4o 31.7. X-Large search space (>10^9): R1 42.5, o1-preview 28.5, o1-mini 17.0, Sonnet 3.5 1.0, 405B 0.0. Small (<10^3): o1-preview 98.4.
limits: Puzzles are single-answer logic grids only; hidden CoT of o1 is not visible.
agent_relevance: Our agent should expect collapse when the number of interacting constraints grows, and must hand large instances to code (O4 propagation done by a solver), not to free-text reasoning.

source: Lin et al. (2025) ZebraLogic: test-time compute on Zebra puzzles
finding: More samples, voting and self-verification help on easy and medium puzzles but barely on large ones. Oracle selection among many samples is far better than any non-oracle selector.
numbers: GPT-4o overall 31.7. Majority vote N=32: 38.0 (Small 98.4, Medium 81.1, Large 28.0, X-Large 2.5). Reward-model best-of-32: 34.8. Self-verify: 32.1. Oracle best-of-32: 60.3; oracle best-of-128: 69.1 (above o1-mini 59.7). o1 models use about 5,100-5,350 hidden reasoning tokens per puzzle vs 503-544 for GPT-4o-mini and GPT-4o.
limits: Oracle numbers are pass@k, an upper bound, not a usable method. Voting is weak because samples share errors.
agent_relevance: Supports G4 and G5: voting from one model gives small gains; a code check (a CSP verifier is cheap) is what turns pass@k into real accuracy.

source: Amonkar et al. (2026) A Reality Check of Language Models as Formalizers on Constraint Satisfaction Problems
finding: Having the LLM write a formal program for a solver (formalizer) does not beat letting it reason to the answer (solver) on real CSPs. Formalizer wins in only 9 of 24 model-dataset cells.
numbers: 4 benchmarks (Calendar Scheduling, Meeting Planning, Trip Planning, ZebraLogic), 6 LLMs, Python vs SMT (Z3). Formalizer underperforms solver in 15 of 24 combinations (12 of 16 reasoning models, 4 of 8 non-reasoning). Python beat SMT in 15 of 24 combinations.
limits: Weakest model (Qwen2.5) did better as formalizer than as solver. Revision-by-error (up to 5 tries) helps in many cells but costs more calls.
agent_relevance: Do not assume 'write a CSP model' is a free win. Use it where the constraint list is long and extraction is easy to check; keep a direct-solve fallback.

source: Amonkar et al. (2026) formalizer scaling and failure analysis
finding: Formalization does not scale with constraint count either, even though solver search is delegated. Most errors are wrongly written constraints, which solver error messages cannot catch.
numbers: With Python and revision, accuracy on the 20% of problems with most constraints is under half that of the 20% with fewest in 10 of 12 model-dataset cells. Manual audit of 80 semantic errors: wrong constraint was the main class (95% for Qwen3); examples are start vs end time, 9:16 vs 9:18.
limits: Manual annotation, small sample (5 per cell).
agent_relevance: A translation check is needed (G3): restate each constraint back in words and compare with the source text, in code, before running the solver.

source: Amonkar et al. (2026) reasoning traces of formalizers
finding: Reasoning models asked to write a program often reason like a solver instead, enumerating and backtracking in the thinking text, and sometimes hard-code the answer into the program.
numbers: Annotated 160 reasoning chains (10 per domain per formalism): under 75% of Qwen3 chains and under 50% of DeepSeek-R1 chains were mainly code-related. Solver-like reasoning used over 1.5 times the tokens of code-related reasoning. Unnecessary reasoning is up to 90% of DeepSeek-R1 programs in all domains.
limits: Small manual sample.
agent_relevance: A scaffold that forces 'declare variables, domains, constraints only' in a template slot may reduce wasted solving-in-the-head; check code for hard-coded answers.

source: Seely et al. (2025) Sudoku-Bench: Evaluating creative reasoning with Sudoku variants
finding: Hard Sudoku variants need a creative break-in (a first non-obvious deduction). Frontier LLMs without tools solve under 15% of the set.
numbers: 100 puzzles (15 4x4, 15 6x6, 70 9x9). Single-shot solve rate overall: o3-mini-high 14.0, Gemini 2.5 Pro 11.0, Qwen3-235B 8.0, DeepSeek R1 6.0, Claude 3.7 Sonnet thinking 5.0, GPT-4.1 2.0. 4x4 solve 40-73% for top models; 9x9 almost 0 (o3-mini-high 2.9 single-shot). Multi-step mode (board returned each turn) gave Gemini 2.5 Pro 11.0 overall.
quote: Without tool use, the evaluation specifically assesses the model's intrinsic reasoning capabilities
limits: Text-only board format; no tools in the baseline. Authors say tool use (solver) makes standard variants easy.
agent_relevance: Constraint propagation by hand fails on unusual interacting constraints. Interactive feedback of the board state did not help on large grids, so the weakness is search and insight, not only state tracking.

source: Seely et al. (2025) Sudoku-Bench: model search behaviour vs human
finding: Models fail to narrow the search space the way human experts do and fall back on brute-force guessing. No tested model found the break-in of the showcased puzzle.
numbers: Expert human found the break-in of one puzzle in about 4.5 minutes and solved it in about 35 minutes; no tested model found that break-in. Gemini 2.5 Pro attempt on Ascension relied on brute-force search.
limits: Case study, single puzzle; qualitative.
agent_relevance: Human CSP solvers use strong propagation rules (naked pairs, etc). Our O4 could offer a rule library, but showing that the model picks the right rule is hard.

source: Stechly, Marquez, Kambhampati (2023) GPT-4 Doesn't Know It's Wrong: iterative prompting on graph coloring
finding: On graph coloring (a CSP), GPT-4 is bad at solving, and bad at verifying its own answers, so self-critique loops fail. The gains from backprompting come mostly from having more tries.
numbers: 100 instances. No backprompt: 16% correct. GPT-4 self-critique loop (up to 15 iterations): 1 of 100 correct. Sound external verifier: about 40%, but binary feedback, one-edge feedback and full-error feedback were not significantly different. Plain resampling n=15 at temperature 1.0 also about 40%. With a sound verifier the model fixed the listed edge in 94-98% of backprompts, yet overall accuracy stayed near 40%.
quote: the correctness and content of the criticisms ... seems largely irrelevant
limits: GPT-4 only (2023); small graphs; one domain.
agent_relevance: Strong support for G2: revise only from real checker output, and note that even then the content of feedback matters less than the number of tries. Budget resampling against a code verifier.

source: Stechly, Valmeekam, Kambhampati (2024) On the Self-Verification Limitations of LLMs on Reasoning and Planning Tasks
finding: Across Game of 24, graph coloring and STRIPS planning, GPT-4 self-critique lowers accuracy; sound external verification helps; sampling alone gives comparable gains to feedback.
numbers: Table 1 (accuracy): graph coloring standard prompting 16%, LLM+LLM critique 2%, LLM with sound verifier 34-40% depending on feedback variant. Game of 24: 5% standard, 3% LLM+LLM, 36-38% with sound verifier.
limits: GPT-4 era models (2024); table columns partly garbled in text extraction, so only the headline cells are recorded.
agent_relevance: Confirms that a code verifier, not the model, should judge CSP solutions. Also warns that loop gain may be mere re-sampling, so compare against equal-budget resampling.

source: Ye et al. (2023) SatLM: Satisfiability-Aided Language Models Using Declarative Prompting
finding: LLM writes declarative constraints (variables, domains, constraints) and a SAT/SMT solver does the search. This beats chain-of-thought and imperative program-aided prompting on logic tasks.
numbers: code-davinci-002 greedy: LSAT SatLM 35.0 vs CoT 23.5; BoardgameQA 79.4 vs 60.7; CLUTRR 68.3 vs ProgLM 58.9; ProofWriter 99.7 vs 83.7; GSM-Sys 69.4 vs CoT 46.5 and ProgLM 43.4; regex 44.0 vs 37.1. With self-consistency SatLM new SoTA: LSAT 37.4 (was 30.9), BoardgameQA 80.7 (was 73.9). GSM-Sys gain over ProgLM about 23%.
limits: GSM greedy is on par with ProgLM (71.8 vs 72.7). Old Codex model.
agent_relevance: Our O4 can be a declarative restate step plus a solver. The ablation below shows the solver itself is the key part.

source: Ye et al. (2023) SatLM ablation: solver vs declarative prompting
finding: Declarative prompting alone, without the solver, is no better than standard prompting. The solver guarantees correct planning and execution. For the CoT solver, planning errors are a large share on hard sets.
numbers: Declarative then answer with no solver was about equal to STANDARD prompting. CoT-solver error split: GSM-Sys plan errors 72.5% / execution errors 27.5%; GSM 42.5/57.5; CLUTRR 47.5/52.5.
limits: Small error-annotation sample; old model.
agent_relevance: Where the check is formal, hand the search to code. Free-text 'think through the constraints' leaves a large plan-error share.

source: Yao et al. (2023) Tree of Thoughts: Mini Crosswords (a CSP with 10 clues)
finding: 5x5 mini crosswords as search with state evaluation, pruning of 'impossible' partial fills, and DFS backtracking. Backtracking and pruning matter. This is propagation-like pruning inside an LLM loop.
numbers: GPT-4. IO and CoT word-level success under 16%. ToT word-level 60%, solves 4 of 20 games. Oracle best DFS state: 7 of 20. Without pruning: generally worse, though it solved 4 of 20 (3 that ToT with pruning could not solve in 100 steps). Without backtracking (greedy, overwrites allowed, 20 steps): word-level 20%.
limits: 20 games only; the state evaluator wrongly pruned valid rare words GPT-4 did not know; GPT-4 (2023).
agent_relevance: A pruning step is a noisy domain-wipe-out test. When the pruner is wrong the correct answer is lost, so keep pruned branches recoverable (restart rather than hard delete).

source: Regin, De Maria, Bonlarron (2024) Combining Constraint Programming Reasoning with LLM Predictions (GenCP)
finding: Text generation under hard constraints is cast as a CSP. The LLM proposes domains (candidate words) on the fly and CP search with backtracking enforces the constraints. It reaches 100% constraint satisfaction where LLMs alone often fail.
numbers: Plain LLMs (GPT-4, GPT-4o, Mistral Next, Claude 3.5, Gemini; 10 trials each) on COLLIE-style sentence tasks: satisfaction rates around 0-10% on counting-style sentence tasks and 90-100% on the easiest lexical task. GenCP satisfaction 100% on the reported tasks. Beam search was slower and less successful; larger beam width did not guarantee more solutions.
limits: Small benchmark, Java prototype, a few tasks; results given per task and not averaged.
agent_relevance: A working LLM+CP loop: the model fills domains, code does propagation and backtracking. Good template for any constraint the model cannot count (length, forbidden letters).

source: Bonlarron, Regin, De Maria, Regin (2025) Large Language Model Meets Constraint Propagation (IJCAI 2025)
finding: Adds a masked language model to GenCP to preview future domains, giving bidirectional propagation. It reduces LLM calls and finds more solutions on strongly constrained tasks.
numbers: COLLIE tasks: sent-1 vanilla 444 LLM calls, 375 backtracks, 3 solutions; meta-variable 456 calls, 211 backtracks, 4 solutions; previewMLM 359 calls, 170 backtracks, 10 solutions (+32 MLM calls). para-2: 3 solutions vs 6 with preview. para-4: 0 solutions vs 2.
limits: Preview depth d=2 on the last two variables only; d=3 or 4 gave fewer solutions in the same time. MLM predicts about 15% masked tokens.
agent_relevance: Look-ahead filtering before assigning (forward checking) reduces both cost and backtracks for LLM-filled domains. Do not over-extend the look-ahead depth.

source: Voboril, Peruvemba Ramaswamy, Szeider (2025) Generating Streamlining Constraints with Large Language Models (JAIR)
finding: LLM proposes extra constraints (streamliners) for MiniZinc models, tested on easy instances and fed back. Some cut solving time by up to 99%. It still worked on disguised and obfuscated problems, which argues against pure memorization.
numbers: 7 CSPs, GPT-4o and Claude 3.5 Sonnet, static vs adaptive prompting, two runs. Reductions of 98% or more on CS, SG and HC problems in some runs; many test instances solved in under 1 second after streamlining. Combinations of streamliners often beat single ones.
limits: Streamliners may remove all solutions; they are checked only on test instances; gains vary by problem.
agent_relevance: LLM as generator of search-space reducers, code as empirical gate (G3: validate on instances it was not fitted to). A model-in-the-loop heuristic for O4.

source: Szeider (2025) MCP-Solver: Integrating Language Models with Constraint Programming Systems
finding: A tool server (Model Context Protocol) that gives an LLM access to MiniZinc, PySAT and Z3 with an edit-and-validate loop on the model, so the model can refine a constraint model step by step.
numbers: No benchmark numbers. Authors state the experiments are 'not rigorous benchmarks'; three transcripts shown (TSP on Austrian provinces, 6 queens plus 5 knights, processor parity check) with Claude Desktop.
limits: Demonstration only; no accuracy measurement.
agent_relevance: A ready pattern for an agent loop: model edits items of a constraint model; the program validates each edit before it is kept.

source: Shi et al. (2025) ConstraintLLM: A Neuro-Symbolic Framework for Industrial-Level Constraint Programming
finding: A 32B model fine-tuned for CP modelling (PyCSP3 + Choco) with constraint-aware retrieval of similar solved models, self-correction from solver errors and tree-of-thought search. It outperforms baselines about 2x on a new industrial benchmark.
numbers: IndusCP: 140 NP-hard instances. One-shot CoT of Qwen2.5-Coder-32B: 23.3% solving accuracy on IndusCP. Abstract: 'outperforms the baselines by 2x'. Other benchmarks: NL4OPT, LGPs, LogicDeduction. 20-second solver limit; trained on 3 A6000 GPUs with QLoRA.
limits: Results table was garbled in text extraction; only the 23.3% baseline and the 2x claim are recorded with confidence. Needs training.
agent_relevance: Retrieval of similar solved constraint models (a case base) plus error-fed repair improves modelling; relevant to a memory of solved constraint patterns.

source: Michailidis, Tsouros, Guns (2025/2026) CP-Bench / DCP-Bench-Open: Evaluating LLMs for Constraint Modelling
finding: Benchmark of discrete combinatorial problems turned into executable models in MiniZinc, CPMpy and OR-Tools. High-level Python frameworks beat the domain-specific language. Sampling plus self-verification raise accuracy a lot.
numbers: Zero-shot single-instance accuracy: Python frameworks up to 75% vs maximum 57.3% for MiniZinc. With inference-time methods up to 91% (gpt-5.1, CPMpy). CPMpy gpt-5.1 70.1% to 90.2%; Kimi-K2 66.5% to 89.0%; MiniZinc gpt-5.1 37.8% to 73.2%. Strict multi-instance accuracy is lower: SIA 78.3% vs MIA 60.9%; gpt-oss-120b and Qwen3-Coder SIA 69.6% to MIA 47.8%. Sampling and self-verification gave over 10-point gains for all LLMs; reasoning mode alone sometimes dropped 5-10 points; retrieval ICL was inconsistent.
limits: Version 1 reported 65% (Python), 50% (DSL) and 70% best; v3 numbers differ because the benchmark changed. Accuracy is solution-level on test instances.
agent_relevance: Checking a model on several instances (G3: not just the one example) exposes a 17-30% relative drop. Self-verification works here because a solver gives ground truth on instances.

source: Cai, Kadioglu, Dilkina (2025) GALA: Global LLM Agents for Text-to-Model Translation
finding: Several agents each detect and write one global-constraint type (all_different, count, etc), then an assembler builds the MiniZinc model. Small gains over CoT.
numbers: Text2Zinc execution / solve rate: o3-mini GALA 57.27% / 32.73% vs CoT 52.73% / 30.91%; gpt-4o-mini GALA 33.64% / 17.27% vs CoT 31.82% / 12.73%; gpt-oss:20b GALA 17.27% / 8.18% vs CoT 16.36% / 10.00% (baseline 11.81% / 7.27%). Detection rate of a global constraint about 70-80%.
limits: Initial experiments, gains of 1-5 points and not always positive; false detection is a risk.
agent_relevance: Decomposing by constraint type is a modest, not large, gain. A checklist of global constraints (O4) may help recall but does not fix mistakes.

source: Wei et al. (2025) SATBench: Benchmarking LLMs' Logical Reasoning via Automated Puzzle Generation from SAT Formulas
finding: 2,100 puzzles from SAT formulas, SAT and UNSAT. Models are decent at finding a satisfying assignment but near chance at proving no assignment exists.
numbers: o4-mini: overall 89.3%; hard UNSAT 65.0% (random 50%); hard SAT 91.1%; hard overall 78.0%. DeepSeek-R1 87.8%, DeepSeek-V3 84.0%. Average over all models on hard problems 53.0%, near random. Clauses: easy 4-19, medium 20-30, hard 31-50. Error types include satisfiability bias, condition omission (o4-mini 14.3%, R1 12.6%) and context inconsistency.
limits: Puzzles are LLM-written stories from CNF; human validation on a subset (pass rate over 90%).
agent_relevance: A CSP agent must not treat 'I found no solution' as proof. Claims of infeasibility need a solver or a certificate (G3, G6).

source: Utsho et al. (2026) Empirical Evidence of Complexity-Induced Limits in LLMs on Finite Discrete State-Space Problems
finding: Nine parameterized puzzles including SAT, cryptarithmetic, graph coloring and Sudoku with deterministic validators. Reasoning models show a phase-transition-like collapse past a task-specific complexity threshold.
numbers: Accuracy drops of often over 50% past thresholds; longer reasoning did not reliably raise correctness; gains in one task family did not transfer. Constraint-dense tasks (Sudoku, coloring) and high-branching tasks collapse early. Failure modes: constraint violations, loss of state tracking, confidently wrong answers.
limits: Exact per-model numbers are in figures; only the text claims were recorded.
agent_relevance: Collapse is sharp, so an agent needs a complexity gate: past a measured size, switch from free reasoning to solver code or decomposition.

source: Srivastava et al. (2026, ICLR) BeyondBench: Contamination-Resistant Evaluation of Reasoning in Language Models
finding: Hard Suite includes Sudoku, N-Queens, graph coloring, SAT. Giving the model the algorithm in the prompt barely helps. Tool use helps but not to ceiling.
numbers: GPT-OSS-120B without vs with explicit algorithm description: Sudoku 9x9 8.2% to 12.1%; N-Queens n=8 22.3% to 28.7%; Boolean SAT (5 vars) 38.1% to 42.8%; Tower of Hanoi n=7 18.4% to 24.2%. With full code access models reach only 67.2% on Sudoku and 58.4% on logic grid puzzles; symbolic solvers (pysat, python-constraint) 68-72% on hard tasks.
limits: Table 5 is from one model (GPT-OSS-120B); appendix failure-mode claims not checked line by line.
agent_relevance: Telling the model the right algorithm (backtracking with propagation) is not enough; it cannot execute it reliably, so the program must run the algorithm.

source: Stojanovski et al. (2025) Reasoning Gym: Reasoning Environments for RL with Verifiable Rewards
finding: Over 100 procedurally generated tasks with verifiers, including constraint-satisfaction games (sudoku, mini sudoku, n_queens, zebra puzzles, cryptarithm) and graph colouring. RL on these tasks raises performance and transfers partly.
numbers: Games-trained models gained +21.8% on algebra and +13.1% on cognition in transfer, which the authors attribute to constraint-satisfaction skills. Curriculum beat non-curriculum in all environments; for example +13.33% for 8-10 empty cells on Mini Sudoku.
limits: Training study (model weights change), not a scaffold; in-domain games performance was poor.
agent_relevance: We do not train, but these verifiable generators can serve as a cheap test suite for our CSP operator (difficulty is adjustable).

source: Dechter (2003) Constraint Processing; Mackworth (1977) Consistency in networks of relations (AC-3)
finding: Core theory: arc consistency, path consistency, k-consistency, backtracking with look-ahead, tree-width decomposition. Propagation prunes domains without search; strong enough consistency on tree-structured networks gives backtrack-free search.
numbers: Not read this session; no numbers recorded.
limits: Background only; claims from memory, not verified here.
agent_relevance: Source of the terms and operators we map to O4 (propagate) and S4.

source: Hao et al. (2025) specific-purpose formalization pipelines for planning (cited by Amonkar et al.)
finding: Cited in the reality-check paper as a special-purpose LLM-to-formal-language pipeline that the authors deliberately did not test.
numbers: No numbers seen.
limits: Only the citation was read; the paper itself was not opened.
agent_relevance: Lead for a later pass if we want a stronger formalizer baseline.

source: Pan et al. (2023) Logic-LM (as cited and reproduced in ConstraintLLM)
finding: Logic-LM translates a problem into symbolic form and runs a solver with self-refinement; ConstraintLLM lists it as previous work on LogicDeduction.
numbers: Not opened itself. The ConstraintLLM table marks it as a result copied from its paper; the exact cell was not reliably extracted.
limits: Secondary mention only.
agent_relevance: Prior art for the translate-then-solve pattern that the reality-check paper questions.

source: Search result (WebSearch, 2026) diffusion vs autoregressive models on Sudoku (arXiv 2601.15593, 2604.24832)
finding: A snippet reports diffusion language models do better than autoregressive ones on Sudoku because they can fill cells in flexible order, which resembles propagating most certain cells first.
numbers: Snippet: fine-tuned Dream-7B score 80 within 10 epochs; Qwen3-8B 15 at 10 epochs, 55 at 50 epochs; 50 train and 100 test samples.
limits: Search snippet only; the papers were not opened.
agent_relevance: Hint that assignment order (most-constrained-first) is what an autoregressive scaffold lacks; code can supply it.
